Model speeds are 80ms for minimal context, 250ms for 32k, 660ms for 100k, and 2.5 seconds for 384k.

text:
if i remember correctly, subq once announced a model with a 12M-token context window and some jaw-dropping benchmarks... then it seemingly vanished from the conversation 👀

hope snap doesn't follow the same...

sure, subq snap beats jev on several benchmarks, especially context window size (sounds familiar, doesn't it?)

but here's the funny part:

- when2call: 67.0 vs jev's 74.6
- api-bank: 86.4 vs jev's 88.0

these aren't random benchmarks, they're directly related to how agents decide what to do next

and the pricing? jev is actually cheaper at $0.042/m input tokens vs snap's $0.05/m

so yeah, impressive numbers, but i'd rather see how it performs in real agent workflows before declaring a winner

if subq snap's outcome is actually more accuracy, that pricing is still a good trade-off

text:
I have 32 tabs open in Chrome right now.

Research, work, that one tweet I'm "getting back to," 3 different ChatGPT sessions, and maybe 8 I don't remember opening.

So I built a Chrome extension that organizes all of them for me.

It's called SnapTab, and it runs on SubQ Snap, a new decision model from Subquadratic @subquadratic that handles small, structured calls faster and cheaper than an LLM. I got early access, and this was the first thing I wanted to build with it.

Open the extension and it shows you every tab, every group you've made, and every duplicate quietly eating your memory.

Then you hit Analyze.

That one click sends your tabs to a local Python server running Snap. The model reads every title and URL and figures out what each tab actually is. Research. Dev. Entertainment. Work.

Hit Organize, and Chrome snaps them into clean groups instantly.

I didn't send any of this to an LLM. Snap has a 384k context window, 12x larger than other decision models, so it can hold your entire browser session in one shot and still cost pennies.

- Finds relevant moments based on your questions
- Shows timestamps so you can jump straight to the answer
- Identifies key topics and suggests chapters
- Saves you from manually scrubbing through hour-long videos

The interesting part is what's powering it.

Subquadratic Snap handles the AI classification, with a 384K-token context window.

You shouldn't have to watch an entire video to find the part that matters.
